stem: The chapter 'An Empire Across Three Continents' deals mainly with the:
options: Roman Empire (and to some extent its contemporary, the Iranian/Parthian empire)
solution: The chapter deals mainly with the Roman Empire, one of the greatest empires of the ancient world, which spread across three continents — Europe, Asia (West Asia), and Africa (North Africa) — around the Mediterranean Sea. It also refers to its contemporary rival, the Iranian (Parthian and later Sasanian) empire.

stem: The Roman Empire spread across which three continents?
solution: The Roman Empire spread across three continents — Europe, Asia (West Asia/the Near East), and Africa (North Africa) — encircling the Mediterranean Sea, which was at the heart of the empire.

stem: The sea that lay at the heart of the Roman Empire, around which its territories were arranged, was the:
solution: The Mediterranean Sea lay at the heart of the Roman Empire; the empire's territories were arranged around this sea, which the Romans called 'Mare Nostrum' ('Our Sea'). The Mediterranean was vital for communication, trade, and the unity of the empire.

stem: The two powerful empires that dominated the region (Europe and West Asia) in this period, ruling much of the world between them, were the Roman Empire and the:
solution: The two great powers of this period were the Roman Empire (around the Mediterranean) and the Iranian Empire (ruled successively by the Parthians and then the Sasanians) to the east; the two empires were rivals and often at war along their shared frontier, and between them they ruled much of Europe and West Asia.

stem: The Roman Empire is broadly divided by historians into two phases: the 'early empire' and the:
solution: Historians broadly divide the history of the Roman Empire (after the end of the Republic) into two main phases — the 'early empire' (from the 1st century onwards, a period of relative stability and prosperity) and the 'late empire' (from roughly the 4th century, a period of significant change, including major reforms and, in the west, eventual decline). (Before the empire, Rome had been a Republic.)

stem: Before it became an empire ruled by emperors, Rome was a:
options: Monarchy under a single king throughout
Republic, governed by the Senate and elected magistrates
solution: Before it became an empire ruled by emperors, Rome was a Republic (from 509 BCE), governed by the Senate (a body of the aristocratic elite) and by elected magistrates (such as the consuls). The Republic lasted for several centuries before giving way, in the 1st century BCE, to rule by emperors (the empire).

stem: The first emperor of Rome, who established one-man rule after the end of the Republic, was:
solution: Augustus (originally Octavian), who came to power after a period of civil war, is regarded as the first emperor of Rome; he established one-man rule (the 'principate') in 27 BCE, marking the transition from Republic to Empire, while maintaining the outward forms of the Republic. His reign began a long period of relative peace and stability.

stem: The three main 'players' or institutions in the political history of the Roman Empire were the emperor, the aristocracy, and the:
solution: The three main 'players' in Roman imperial politics were the emperor, the aristocracy (the Senate and the elite), and the army. The balance and relationship among these three — especially the crucial role and power of the army (whose support the emperor depended on) — were central to the politics and stability of the empire.

stem: The Roman army was a professional, paid army, which meant that:
options: Soldiers were full-time professionals who received a salary (wages) and served for fixed terms, forming a permanent standing army
solution: The Roman army was a professional, paid, standing army: its soldiers were full-time professionals who received regular wages (salary) and served for fixed terms of service. This large, permanent, professional army was one of the pillars of the empire — essential for defence, conquest, and the maintenance of order — and its loyalty and support were vital to the emperors (who had to keep the army satisfied).

stem: The Roman Senate was a body that represented the interests of:
options: The wealthy, aristocratic elite (the upper classes)
solution: The Senate was a body that represented the interests of the wealthy, aristocratic elite (the upper classes) of Rome. It had been the leading institution of the Republic, and it continued to have importance and prestige under the empire, though real power came to rest with the emperor. The relationship between the emperor and the Senate/aristocracy was an important feature of Roman imperial politics.

stem: The Roman Empire was culturally diverse, marked by a diversity of:
options: Languages, religions, and social customs among its many different peoples across three continents
solution: The Roman Empire was culturally very diverse, encompassing a great variety of languages (though Latin and Greek were the main languages of administration and culture), religions (many local gods and cults, before the later spread of Christianity), and social customs among its many different peoples spread across three continents. This cultural diversity was a striking feature of the empire, which brought together many different peoples and traditions under a single political system.

stem: The two main languages of administration and culture in the Roman Empire were:
solution: The two main languages of administration and culture in the Roman Empire were Latin (dominant in the western half of the empire) and Greek (dominant in the eastern half); the empire was, in this sense, bilingual at the level of its administration and elite culture. Latin was the language of the Roman state and army, while Greek was the language of culture and administration in the east.

stem: The economy of the Roman Empire featured well-developed:
options: Trade, agriculture, mining, and manufacture, connected by a network of roads, sea routes, and a common currency
Isolated village economies with no exchange
solution: The Roman Empire had a well-developed and integrated economy, featuring extensive trade (across the Mediterranean and beyond), productive agriculture, mining, and manufacture (of goods like pottery, textiles, and metalwork), all connected by an excellent network of roads, sea routes (across the Mediterranean), harbours, and a common currency (coinage). This economic integration and prosperity, especially during the early empire, was a notable feature of Roman civilisation.

stem: Roman society and economy depended significantly on the labour of:
options: Slaves, who were widely used in agriculture, mines, households, and many other areas
solution: Roman society and economy depended significantly on slavery: slaves (often prisoners of war, but also others) were widely used as labour in agriculture (on large estates), in mines, in households, in crafts and industry, and in many other areas. Slavery was an important and pervasive institution in the Roman world, and the labour of slaves was fundamental to the Roman economy and to the lifestyle of the wealthy — though slavery declined somewhat in the later empire.

stem: Which of the following was an important feature of the Roman Empire that helped hold it together?
options: A common system of law, a network of roads, a common coinage, and effective administration and army
solution: Several features helped hold the vast and diverse Roman Empire together: a common system of Roman law; an excellent network of roads (and sea routes) that facilitated communication, trade, and the movement of armies; a common coinage (currency) that facilitated trade and taxation; an effective system of administration (with provinces, governors, and cities); and a powerful, professional army that defended the frontiers and maintained order. These integrating features — law, roads, coinage, administration, and army — were among the great achievements of the Roman Empire and were crucial to maintaining its unity and stability across three continents.

stem: Roman law and the Roman legal tradition are important because they:
options: Developed a sophisticated body of law and legal principles that had a lasting influence on later legal systems in Europe and beyond
solution: Roman law and the Roman legal tradition are of great importance because the Romans developed a sophisticated, well-organised body of law and legal principles (covering areas such as property, contracts, rights, and procedures), which had a profound and lasting influence on the legal systems of later Europe (and, through them, of much of the world). Roman law is regarded as one of the great and enduring achievements and legacies of Roman civilisation.

stem: The period of relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire, especially during the early empire, is sometimes referred to as:
solution: The long period of relative peace, stability, and prosperity across the Roman Empire, especially during the early empire (roughly the first two centuries CE), is sometimes referred to as the 'Pax Romana' (the 'Roman Peace'). During this period, the empire enjoyed internal stability, flourishing trade and cities, and relative security within its frontiers — one of the notable achievements of the Roman imperial system.

stem: Cities were an important feature of the Roman Empire; a Roman city typically had public amenities such as:
options: Baths, amphitheatres, aqueducts (for water supply), markets, temples, and public buildings
solution: Cities were an important and characteristic feature of the Roman Empire, and a typical Roman city was provided with impressive public amenities and buildings — such as public baths, amphitheatres and theatres (for entertainment and spectacles), aqueducts (to supply water), markets (fora), temples, and other public buildings and monuments. These urban amenities reflect the developed urban civilisation, engineering skill, and public life of the Roman world, and the importance of cities in Roman civilisation.

stem: Roman engineering achievements included the construction of:
options: Roads, bridges, aqueducts, and large public buildings, using techniques like the arch and concrete
solution: Roman engineering achievements were remarkable and included the construction of an extensive network of durable roads and bridges, aqueducts (to carry water over long distances to cities), harbours, and large and impressive public buildings and monuments — using advanced techniques such as the arch, the vault, the dome, and concrete. Roman engineering and construction were highly advanced for their time, and many Roman structures (like roads, aqueducts, and buildings) survive to this day, testifying to the skill and achievement of Roman engineering.

stem: The religion that gradually spread through the Roman Empire and eventually became its dominant religion was:
solution: Christianity gradually spread through the Roman Empire (from the 1st century CE onwards); initially it was a minority religion and its followers were at times persecuted, but it grew steadily, and in the 4th century it was legalised (under Constantine) and eventually became the official and dominant religion of the empire. The spread and rise of Christianity within the Roman Empire is one of the most important developments of the period and had profound long-term consequences for European and world history.

stem: The Roman emperor who is associated with the legalisation of Christianity (through the Edict of Milan) and the beginning of its rise to dominance was:
solution: The Roman emperor Constantine (early 4th century CE) is associated with the legalisation and promotion of Christianity — through the Edict of Milan (313 CE), which granted toleration to Christians — and with the beginning of Christianity's rise to become the dominant religion of the empire. Constantine himself came to favour and support Christianity, and this imperial support was a major factor in the spread and triumph of Christianity in the Roman world.

stem: In the late empire, the emperor Diocletian and others carried out important:
options: Reforms of the administration, army, and economy, to strengthen and reorganise the empire
solution: In the late empire, emperors such as Diocletian (late 3rd century CE) and Constantine carried out important reforms of the administration, army, and economy — reorganising and strengthening the imperial system in response to the crises and pressures the empire faced. These reforms (including administrative reorganisation, the strengthening and reorganisation of the army, and economic and monetary measures) reshaped the empire in its later phase, though the western part of the empire eventually declined and fell in the 5th century.

stem: The western part of the Roman Empire eventually declined and fell in the 5th century CE, largely due to:
options: A combination of internal problems and pressure/invasions by various Germanic and other tribes from beyond the frontiers
solution: The western part of the Roman Empire eventually declined and fell in the 5th century CE, due to a combination of factors — including internal problems (economic difficulties, administrative and political troubles) and increasing pressure and invasions by various Germanic and other tribes (such as the Goths, Vandals, and others) from beyond the frontiers, who moved into and eventually overran the western provinces. The eastern part of the empire (later known as the Byzantine Empire, centred on Constantinople), however, survived and continued for many more centuries. The fall of the western Roman Empire is a major turning point in European history.

stem: The eastern part of the Roman Empire, which survived after the fall of the west and continued for centuries, had its capital at:
solution: The eastern part of the Roman Empire, which survived after the fall of the western empire and continued for about another thousand years (until 1453), had its capital at Constantinople (formerly Byzantium, and modern Istanbul). This surviving eastern empire is often known to historians as the Byzantine Empire. Constantinople had been founded/refounded as an imperial capital by Constantine, and it became the great centre of the eastern Roman/Byzantine world.

stem: The main sources used by historians to reconstruct the history of the Roman Empire include:
options: Texts (histories, letters, laws, literature), documents (like papyri and inscriptions), coins, and material/archaeological remains
solution: Historians reconstruct the history of the Roman Empire from a rich variety of sources, including: texts (histories written by ancient authors, letters, speeches, laws, and literary works); documentary evidence (such as papyri — documents written on papyrus, especially from Egypt — and inscriptions on stone and other materials); coins (which provide information on emperors, economy, and propaganda); and material and archaeological remains (buildings, monuments, artefacts, and the remains of cities). This wealth and variety of sources makes the Roman Empire one of the best-documented and most thoroughly studied of ancient civilisations.

stem: The overall significance of the Roman Empire in world history lies in the fact that it:
options: Was one of the greatest empires in history, which united a vast and diverse region for centuries and left a lasting legacy in law, language, engineering, administration, and (through Christianity) religion
Was a small and unimportant state
solution: The overall significance of the Roman Empire in world history lies in its being one of the greatest and most influential empires in history: it united a vast and culturally diverse region across three continents (around the Mediterranean) under a single political system for several centuries, and it left a profound and lasting legacy — in law (Roman law, which influenced later legal systems), language (Latin, the ancestor of the Romance languages and a language of learning), engineering and architecture (roads, aqueducts, the arch, concrete), administration and governance, urban civilisation, and — through the spread and eventual dominance of Christianity within the empire — religion. The influence of Rome on later European and world civilisation, in these and other respects, has been immense and enduring, which is why the Roman Empire holds such an important place in the study of world history.

stem: The role of the army in Roman imperial politics was crucial because:
options: The emperor depended on the army's support and loyalty to gain and hold power, and the army could make or unmake emperors
solution: The role of the army in Roman imperial politics was crucial because the emperor fundamentally depended on the support and loyalty of the army to gain and hold power; a professional, paid, standing army was the backbone of the empire, and its backing was essential to any emperor. Consequently, the army could 'make or unmake' emperors — the support of the army (or a section of it) could raise a man to the throne, and its disaffection or rebellion could bring an emperor down. Emperors therefore had to keep the army satisfied (with pay, rewards, and successful leadership). This central role and power of the army — and the emperor's dependence on it — was a defining and sometimes destabilising feature of Roman imperial politics, and it was especially evident in periods of crisis when rival claimants, backed by different armies, fought for the throne.

stem: The Roman family and household structure was typically:
options: Patriarchal, with the father (paterfamilias) as the head, holding authority over the household
solution: The Roman family and household were typically patriarchal, headed by the father — the 'paterfamilias' (father/head of the family) — who held authority (legally very extensive in early Roman law) over the members of the household, including his wife, children, and slaves. The patriarchal family, headed by the paterfamilias, was an important social institution in Roman society, though the position and rights of women and the nature of family relationships evolved over the long history of Rome. Understanding the patriarchal structure of the Roman family gives insight into the social organisation and values of Roman society.

stem: Which of the following statements about the Roman economy is correct?
options: It was a simple, isolated, non-monetary economy
It was a complex, monetised, and interconnected economy with extensive trade, specialised production, and the use of coinage across the empire
solution: The Roman economy was a complex, monetised, and interconnected economy — not a simple, isolated, or purely barter economy. It featured extensive trade (across the Mediterranean and beyond, in goods such as grain, wine, olive oil, pottery, textiles, and luxury items), specialised regional production (with different areas specialising in particular goods), productive agriculture (including large estates), mining and manufacture, and the widespread use of coinage (a common currency) that facilitated trade, taxation, and payment throughout the empire. The empire's excellent network of roads and sea routes, common currency, and relative peace (especially during the early empire) supported a high degree of economic integration, exchange, and prosperity across its vast territories. This complex, monetised, and interconnected economy was a notable achievement and feature of the Roman Empire, and it underpinned the prosperity of its cities and the wealth of its elite. (The degree of economic development and prosperity varied over time and place, and the economy faced difficulties, especially in the later empire, but the overall picture is of a sophisticated and interconnected economy for its time.)

stem: The Iranian empire that was the great rival of Rome to the east was first the Parthian and later the:
solution: The great Iranian empire to the east, which was the principal rival of Rome, was ruled first by the Parthians and later (from the 3rd century CE) by the Sasanians (Sassanids). The Sasanian empire was a powerful and sophisticated state that rivalled Rome for control of the frontier regions of West Asia, and the two empires — Roman and Sasanian — were often at war along their shared frontier. The rivalry between the Roman and Iranian (Parthian/Sasanian) empires was a major feature of the geopolitics of this period, and it is referred to in the chapter as part of the wider context of the two great empires of Europe and West Asia.

stem: The transition of the Roman world from the worship of many gods (paganism) to Christianity is an example of a major:
options: Religious and cultural transformation that reshaped the civilisation and had lasting consequences
solution: The transition of the Roman world from polytheism/paganism (the worship of many gods) to Christianity (a monotheistic religion) is an example of a major religious and cultural transformation — one that fundamentally reshaped the civilisation of the Roman world and had profound and lasting consequences for the subsequent history of Europe and the world. Over the course of a few centuries, Christianity spread from being a small and sometimes persecuted minority religion to becoming the official and dominant religion of the empire; this transformation reshaped the religious, cultural, moral, and institutional life of the Roman world, and it laid foundations for the Christian civilisation of medieval and later Europe. The rise and triumph of Christianity within the Roman Empire is thus one of the most significant and consequential transformations of the entire period, and it illustrates how great civilisations can undergo profound religious and cultural change over time.

stem: The extensive network of Roman roads served the important functions of:
options: Facilitating the movement of armies, trade, communication, and administration across the vast empire
solution: The extensive and famous network of Roman roads — durable, well-engineered roads connecting the many parts of the empire — served several important functions: it facilitated the rapid movement of armies (for defence and the maintenance of order), the flow of trade and goods, communication (including the imperial postal/messenger system) and the transmission of news and orders, and the administration of the far-flung provinces. The saying 'all roads lead to Rome' reflects the centrality of Rome in this road network. The Roman road network was thus a vital instrument of the unity, defence, trade, communication, and administration of the empire, and it was one of the great engineering and organisational achievements of Roman civilisation, some of whose roads and routes remained in use for centuries.

stem: Roman citizenship, which had earlier been limited, was extended to all free inhabitants of the empire in 212 CE by the emperor:
solution: In 212 CE, the emperor Caracalla extended Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire (through the Constitutio Antoniniana). Before this, citizenship had been more limited (though it had been gradually extended over time); this measure made virtually all free people of the empire Roman citizens, a significant step in the integration of the empire's diverse populations.

stem: The province of Egypt was especially important to the Roman Empire because it was a major source of:
options: Grain (wheat) — serving as a granary that helped feed the population, especially of the city of Rome
solution: The province of Egypt was especially important to the Roman Empire as a major source of grain (wheat); its fertile Nile valley made it a great granary, and the grain of Egypt (along with that of North Africa) was crucial for feeding the large population of the empire, particularly the city of Rome. Control of Egypt's grain supply was therefore of great strategic and economic importance to the Roman state.

stem: The large amphitheatres of the Roman world, such as the Colosseum in Rome, were used for:
options: Public spectacles and entertainments, including gladiatorial contests and other shows
solution: The large amphitheatres of the Roman world — the most famous being the Colosseum in Rome — were used for public spectacles and mass entertainments, most notably gladiatorial contests (fights between gladiators, or between men and animals), as well as other shows and spectacles. These public entertainments were an important feature of Roman urban and public life, provided to the population (often for free) by the state or the elite. The amphitheatres themselves were remarkable feats of Roman engineering and architecture.

stem: Gladiators in the Roman world were:
options: Fighters (often slaves, prisoners, or the condemned, though sometimes free volunteers) who fought in public spectacles in the amphitheatres
solution: Gladiators were fighters who fought, often to the death, in public spectacles in the amphitheatres for the entertainment of the crowds. They were typically slaves, prisoners of war, or condemned criminals (though some were free volunteers), trained in special schools; gladiatorial games were a popular and characteristic (if brutal) feature of Roman public entertainment. The phenomenon of gladiators and the games illustrates aspects of Roman society, entertainment, and the institution of slavery.

stem: In the Roman family, the position and rights of women:
options: Were completely equal to men in all respects
Were subordinate in law and society (the family being patriarchal), though women — especially of the upper classes — could own property and had some independence and influence
solution: In the Roman family and society, the position of women was generally subordinate to that of men — the family being patriarchal, headed by the paterfamilias — and women were subject to significant legal and social restrictions. However, women (especially of the upper classes) were not without rights or influence: they could own property (an important right), could obtain divorce, managed households, and could exercise some independence and social influence, and the legal position and social role of women evolved over the long history of Rome. So while Roman society was patriarchal and women were legally and socially subordinate to men in important respects, women — particularly of the elite — could own property and had a degree of independence and influence. Understanding the position of women gives insight into Roman social structure, law, and values.

stem: A slave who had been freed by his or her master in the Roman world was known as a:
solution: A slave who had been freed (manumitted) by his or her master was known as a 'freedman' (or 'freedwoman'). The freeing of slaves (manumission) was fairly common in the Roman world, and freedmen — though they often retained certain obligations to their former masters (now their patrons) — became free and could acquire property, engage in business, and (for their descendants) even rise in society. Some freedmen became quite wealthy and successful. The existence of freedmen, and the practice of manumission, was an important feature of the social structure and mobility of the Roman world, and it reflects the workings and complexities of the institution of slavery in Rome.

stem: The main frontiers that the Roman army had to defend were formed largely by the rivers Rhine and Danube in Europe and the frontier with Iran (the Euphrates region) in the east. These frontiers were threatened by:
options: Germanic and other tribes in the north/west, and the Iranian (Parthian/Sasanian) empire in the east
solution: The main land frontiers of the Roman Empire ran largely along the rivers Rhine and Danube in Europe (the northern frontier) and along the frontier with the Iranian empire in the east (the region of the Euphrates). These frontiers were threatened and had to be defended against external enemies: in the north and west, by various Germanic and other tribes (who pressed against and sometimes invaded across the Rhine-Danube frontier); and in the east, by the rival Iranian (Parthian and later Sasanian) empire (along the eastern frontier). Defending these long frontiers against these external threats was one of the main and continuing tasks of the powerful Roman army, and the pressure on the frontiers (especially the invasions of Germanic and other tribes) was a major factor in the eventual difficulties and, in the west, the fall of the empire.

stem: The Roman Empire's currency was based mainly on coins made of:
options: Precious metals — especially the silver coin called the denarius, and gold coins
solution: The Roman Empire's currency was based mainly on coins made of precious metals — especially the silver coin called the denarius, as well as gold coins (like the aureus) and lower-value coins of bronze/copper. This system of metal coinage provided a common currency across the empire, which facilitated trade, taxation, the payment of the army and officials, and economic exchange throughout the vast Roman world. The stability and value of the coinage were important to the economy, and the debasement (reduction in precious-metal content) of the coinage in the later empire, associated with economic and inflationary problems, was one of the difficulties faced by the empire in its later phase. Roman coins are also an important source for historians, providing information about emperors, the economy, and imperial propaganda.

stem: The third century CE was a period of serious crisis for the Roman Empire, marked by:
options: Political instability (rapid turnover of emperors), military pressure on the frontiers, and economic difficulties
solution: The third century CE (particularly the middle decades) was a period of serious crisis for the Roman Empire, marked by: severe political instability (with a rapid succession of many short-lived emperors, often raised up and overthrown by the army, amid civil wars and struggles for the throne); heavy military pressure and invasions on the frontiers (from Germanic tribes in the north and the resurgent Sasanian empire in the east); and economic difficulties (including inflation and the debasement of the coinage). This 'third-century crisis' shook the empire and threatened its stability and survival; it was followed by the major reforms of Diocletian and Constantine (in the late 3rd and early 4th centuries), which reorganised and stabilised the empire for a further period, though the western empire eventually declined and fell in the 5th century. The third-century crisis illustrates the pressures, instability, and difficulties that the empire could face, and the crucial and sometimes destabilising role of the army in imperial politics.

stem: The general prosperity and stability of the early empire depended significantly on:
options: Relative internal peace, effective administration, flourishing trade and agriculture, and the security provided by the army along the frontiers
The absence of any government or army
solution: The general prosperity and stability of the early Roman Empire (the period of the 'Pax Romana') depended significantly on several interrelated factors: relative internal peace and political stability (especially in comparison with the civil wars of the late Republic and the later crisis); effective administration of the provinces; flourishing trade (across the Mediterranean and beyond) and productive agriculture, supported by a common currency, good roads and sea routes, and the integration of the empire's economy; and the security provided by the professional army, which defended the frontiers and maintained order, allowing peaceful economic and civic life to flourish within the empire. Together, these conditions — peace, effective administration, economic prosperity, and military security — underpinned the relative stability, prosperity, and flourishing of the early empire and its cities. The interdependence of these factors also means that when they were disrupted (as in the third-century crisis), the stability and prosperity of the empire were threatened. Understanding the factors underlying the prosperity and stability of the early empire gives insight into the workings and achievements of the Roman imperial system at its height.

stem: The two great cultural zones of the Roman Empire were the Latin-speaking:
solution: The Roman Empire had two great cultural (and linguistic) zones: the Latin-speaking West (the western provinces, including Italy, Gaul, Spain, Britain, and North Africa west of Egypt, where Latin was the dominant language of administration and culture) and the Greek-speaking East (the eastern provinces, including Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, and Egypt, where Greek was the dominant language of administration and high culture, reflecting the earlier spread of Greek civilisation in the region). This division between the Latin West and the Greek East was an important cultural feature of the empire, and it corresponded roughly to the later political division between the western empire (which fell in the 5th century) and the eastern/Byzantine empire (which survived, and in which Greek remained dominant). The bilingual and bicultural character of the empire — Latin West and Greek East — reflects the rich and diverse cultural heritage that Rome brought together and ruled over, and the different cultural traditions of the two halves of the empire.

stem: Papyrus, an important writing material in the Roman world (especially in Egypt), was made from:
options: A reed plant that grew along the Nile
solution: Papyrus, an important writing material in the ancient world (including the Roman world, and especially associated with Egypt), was made from the papyrus reed — a reed plant that grew abundantly along the Nile in Egypt. The pith of the reed was processed into sheets that could be written on, and papyrus was widely used for documents, letters, records, and books. Many papyrus documents have survived (especially in the dry climate of Egypt), and these papyri are a valuable source for historians of the Roman world, providing detailed information about everyday life, administration, economy, and society. The use of papyrus (alongside other materials) illustrates the writing and record-keeping practices of the Roman world, and the survival of papyri contributes to making the Roman Empire one of the well-documented civilisations of antiquity.

stem: Which of the following best describes the Roman attitude that helped integrate conquered peoples into the empire?
options: Complete exclusion of all conquered peoples
A degree of openness — extending Roman citizenship and allowing local elites and peoples to participate in and benefit from the Roman system over time
Total destruction of all local cultures
solution: One of the factors that helped integrate conquered peoples into the Roman Empire was a degree of openness and willingness to incorporate them into the Roman system: over time, Rome extended Roman citizenship to more and more of the empire's inhabitants (culminating in Caracalla's grant of citizenship to all free inhabitants in 212 CE); allowed and encouraged local elites and communities to participate in the administration, army, and civic life of the empire, and to benefit from the Roman system (through trade, citizenship, offices, and the amenities of Roman urban life); and generally tolerated local customs, languages, and religions (before the later dominance of Christianity), while spreading Roman law, language (Latin/Greek), and civic institutions. This relative openness and capacity to integrate and incorporate diverse conquered peoples — extending citizenship, allowing participation, and (to a degree) tolerating local cultures — helped to bind the empire's many peoples into a single political system and to give them a stake in it, contributing to the stability, integration, and durability of the empire. It reflects a notable feature of the Roman imperial system: its ability to incorporate and integrate a great diversity of peoples and cultures into a single, relatively cohesive empire — an important factor in Rome's success and longevity as an imperial power.

stem: The Roman Empire is significant as a subject of study partly because the abundance and variety of its sources allow historians to:
options: Reconstruct many aspects of its history, society, economy, and daily life in considerable detail
solution: The Roman Empire is significant and rewarding as a subject of historical study partly because of the abundance and variety of its surviving sources — texts (histories, letters, laws, literature, speeches), documents (papyri, inscriptions), coins, and rich archaeological and material remains (buildings, monuments, cities, artefacts). This wealth and variety of evidence allows historians to reconstruct many aspects of the empire's history in considerable detail — not only its political and military history and its emperors, but also its administration, economy, trade, social structure, family life, slavery, religion, culture, cities, technology, and the daily life of ordinary people. This makes the Roman Empire one of the best-documented and most thoroughly studied of all ancient civilisations, and it enables a rich, detailed, and many-sided understanding of the workings and life of a great ancient empire. The richness of the sources, and the detailed picture of the empire that they allow historians to reconstruct, is one of the reasons the Roman Empire holds such an important and prominent place in the study of ancient and world history.

stem: The relationship between the emperor and the aristocracy (Senate) in the Roman Empire was:
options: Complex — the emperor held real power, but the aristocracy retained wealth, prestige, and social importance, and emperors generally sought to work with (or at least manage) them
solution: The relationship between the emperor and the aristocracy (represented especially by the Senate) in the Roman Empire was complex and important. With the establishment of the empire, real political power came to rest with the emperor (who controlled the army and the administration), and the political power of the Senate/aristocracy was much reduced compared to the Republic. However, the aristocracy retained great wealth, social prestige, and importance: many senators and aristocrats continued to hold high offices, govern provinces, command armies, and play leading roles in the administration and society of the empire, and the Senate retained considerable prestige and a formal role. Emperors generally sought to work with, honour, and manage the aristocracy (whose cooperation and administrative talents were useful), though relations could be tense or hostile with particular emperors (some of whom clashed with or persecuted senators). The emperor, the aristocracy (Senate), and the army were the three key 'players' in imperial politics, and the balance and relationship among them — including the emperor's management of the aristocracy — was central to the workings and stability of the imperial system. Understanding this complex relationship between the emperor and the aristocracy gives insight into the political structure and dynamics of the Roman Empire.

stem: The spread of Christianity was aided, in part, by:
options: The unity, peace, common languages (Greek and Latin), and good communications (roads and sea routes) of the Roman Empire, which allowed the new religion to spread across its territories
solution: The spread of Christianity across the Roman Empire was aided, in part, by the very features and conditions of the empire itself: its political unity and relative internal peace (which allowed people, ideas, and missionaries to move and communicate across a vast area); its common languages (especially Greek, and also Latin), which allowed the Christian message to be communicated widely; and its excellent network of roads and sea routes and good communications, which facilitated the movement of people (including Christian missionaries like the Apostle Paul) and the spread of ideas across the empire's territories. The urban character of the empire, and the presence of diverse communities in its cities, also provided settings in which the new religion could take root and spread. Thus, the unity, peace, common languages, good communications, and urban network of the Roman Empire helped to create conditions favourable to the spread of Christianity from its origins in the eastern Mediterranean throughout the empire — one of the factors (along with the appeal of the religion itself and, later, imperial support) that contributed to the remarkable spread and eventual triumph of Christianity within the Roman world. This illustrates how the framework and conditions of the empire could facilitate the spread of a new religion, and it is part of the story of the major religious transformation of the Roman world.

stem: The legacy of Latin, the language of the Romans, includes the fact that it:
options: Was the ancestor of the modern Romance languages (like Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian) and long remained a language of learning, law, and the Church in Europe
Is the same as modern English
solution: The legacy of Latin, the language of the Romans and of the western empire, has been immense and enduring. Latin was the ancestor of the modern Romance languages — including Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Romanian — which developed out of the spoken Latin of the different regions of the western empire; these languages are spoken by hundreds of millions of people today. In addition, Latin long remained (for many centuries after the fall of the western empire) a vital language of learning, scholarship, law, administration, and the Christian Church in Europe, and it profoundly influenced the vocabulary and development of other European languages (including English, which has absorbed a great many words of Latin origin). Latin also remained the language of much European literature, science, and record-keeping down to early modern times. The enduring influence and legacy of Latin — as the parent of the Romance languages, and as a long-lived language of learning, law, and the Church — is thus one of the great and lasting contributions of Roman civilisation to the subsequent history and culture of Europe and the world, and it illustrates the deep and continuing influence of Rome on later civilisation. This linguistic legacy is one important example of the many enduring ways in which the Roman Empire shaped the world that came after it.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'An Empire Across Three Continents' is that:
options: The Roman Empire was a vast, diverse, and sophisticated empire that united much of Europe, West Asia, and North Africa for centuries, with a complex economy, effective administration, powerful army, rich culture, and enduring legacy, alongside its great rival the Iranian empire
solution: The chapter conveys that the Roman Empire was a vast, culturally diverse, and highly sophisticated empire that united much of Europe, West Asia, and North Africa — the lands around the Mediterranean — under a single political system for several centuries. It had a complex and monetised economy with extensive trade and specialised production; an effective system of administration, law, and coinage; a powerful, professional standing army (on which the emperors depended); impressive cities, engineering, and public works; and a rich and diverse culture, with Latin and Greek as its main languages. Its history unfolded through phases (the early and late empire), and it faced its great rival in the Iranian (Parthian/Sasanian) empire to the east. Over time, it underwent major transformations — including the rise and eventual triumph of Christianity, important reforms in the late empire, and, in the west, eventual decline and fall in the 5th century (while the eastern/Byzantine empire survived for much longer). The Roman Empire left a profound and enduring legacy — in law, language, engineering, administration, urban civilisation, and religion — that deeply influenced the subsequent history of Europe and the world. The chapter thus presents the Roman Empire as one of the greatest and most influential empires in world history, illustrating the nature, achievements, complexity, and legacy of a great ancient empire spread across three continents.
